h1: Home Power Planner: Free Electricity Calculators
author: ali-ahmad
answer: The Home Power Planner sizes everything from one appliance list: a typical home running {{out.running_w|int}} W needs about a {{out.inverter_kw|up1}} kW inverter, a {{out.battery_ah|up}} Ah battery bank at {{out.battery_v}} V for {{in.backup_hours|1}} hours of backup, a {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW solar system of {{out.panels|int}} panels that saves about {{out.saving_rs|rs}} a month in energy charge under net billing, and a {{out.generator_pick_kva|1}} kVA generator. Edit the list and every size updates.
key_facts: The planner carries one appliance list through the whole chain: running load, inverter, battery, solar, net billing and generator, each with the formula of its own calculator, so the sizes never contradict each other.

Inverter size = running watts × {{d.margin|2}}, raised if needed so the solar array is at most {{d.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} times it; battery Ah = backup watts × hours ÷ (bank volts × usable depth of discharge × inverter efficiency); solar kW = the larger of daily units ÷ city yield and running watts ÷ performance ratio, with net billing counting the array only up to the sanctioned load; generator kVA = the larger of running × {{d.margin|2}} and the starting peak, ÷ {{d.pf_generator|1}}.

Default values (inverter efficiency {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} UPS and {{d.inverter_eff_hybrid|pct}} hybrid, usable battery capacity {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} tubular and {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}} lithium, power factor {{d.pf_mixed|2}}) are listed on the methodology page and editable in each calculator.
Pakistan tariff slabs, peak sun hours by city and appliance wattages live in dated data files; the net-billing buyback rate is not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page and stays editable.
Results are planning estimates, not an official bill or an engineer's design; wiring and solar work must be confirmed by a licensed electrician.

sections.h2: What the planner does, step by step
p: Step one adds up the appliances you tick: the watts that run at once and the units they use in a day. Step two sizes the inverter for that running load with a safety margin, and step four can raise it so the inverter accepts the solar array. Step three sizes the battery for only the load you want to keep on during loadshedding, for the hours you choose. Step four sizes the solar array for your daily units and your city's sun. Step five splits a month's solar between what you use while the sun is up and what you export, and compares the energy charge with and without net billing. Step six sizes a generator for the whole list, in case you want one for long outages.
Every step is a calculator on this site. Open any of them from the task cards below to change its assumptions, see worked examples and read the formula.

Start with the task, not the jargon. If the lights go out during loadshedding, start with the battery and UPS tools. If the bill is the problem, start with the bill calculators and the AC consumption tool. If you are planning solar, add up your home load first, then size the system.

Each result page ends with a Next step link to the tool that naturally follows, so a battery backup time leads to inverter sizing, a home load leads to solar sizing, and a wire size leads to the breaker to pair with it.

sections.h2: Why the numbers can be trusted
p: The calculators share one engine with one set of formulas and one set of constants. The same formula produces the live result, the worked examples, the reference tables and the FAQ answers on every page, so no two pages can disagree.

The formulas follow standard electrical practice (IEC and NEPRA performance standards for a {{d.v_1ph|int}} V, {{d.v_3ph|int}} V three-phase, fifty hertz supply). Assumptions that depend on judgement are marked and editable, and a review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress.

faq.q: Can I save or share my plan?
faq.a: Yes. Press the plan button, then use Save as PDF to print or keep the page, WhatsApp to send the sizes and a link to your installer, or copy the link: it carries your appliance list, so whoever opens it sees the same plan.

faq.q: Why is the saving an energy-charge estimate only?
faq.a: The planner compares only the energy charge of {{out.monthly_units|int}} units with the net-billing energy charge after {{out.self_used_units|int}} self-used and {{out.export_units|int}} exported units. Fixed charge, per-unit surcharges and GST are left out; most of them also fall when you import fewer units, so the real saving is usually somewhat higher than this estimate. The buyback rate is editable because it is not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page.
Yes. Every tool runs in your browser, needs no sign-up and stores nothing about you. You can share a result by copying the page link after you press Calculate.

faq.q: Do the tools work outside Pakistan?
faq.a: Yes. The defaults are set for Pakistan ({{d.v_1ph|int}} V single phase, rupees, local tariff slabs), and the converters, battery, solar and wiring tools let you switch to {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V or enter your own voltage and prices.

They are planning estimates built on typical values. Real backup time, bills and solar output depend on battery age, weather, the exact appliance and the tariff of the month, so expect the real number to land near the estimate, not exactly on it.

faq.q: Who writes and checks the tools?
faq.a: Wattlyst is written by its founder, Ali Ahmad, with formulas documented on the methodology page. Technical review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress and will be named on each page once complete.

fields.name: loads
fields.label: Appliances you run (edit the list)
fields.hint: Watts and hours fill in from our appliance data; change any value to match your home.

fields.name: city
fields.label: City (for sun hours)
fields.hint: Sets the solar yield from Global Solar Atlas data. Pick the nearest city.

fields.name: sanctioned_kw
fields.label: Sanctioned load
fields.hint: The kW printed on your electricity bill. Below five keeps the flat tariff; it also caps net billing.

fields.name: backup_w
fields.label: Load to keep on during loadshedding
fields.hint: Fans, lights, Wi-Fi and TV are a few hundred watts; an inverter AC adds over a thousand.

fields.name: backup_hours
fields.label: Backup hours wanted
fields.hint: The longest outage you want to cover from the battery.

fields.name: buyback_rs
fields.label: Net-billing buyback rate
fields.hint: Not yet confirmed on a NEPRA page; change it when your DISCO quotes a rate.

fields.name: day_share
fields.label: Share of use while the sun is up
fields.hint: How much of the day's electricity you use between sunrise and sunset. Half is typical for a home.

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Sizing margin
fields.hint: Inverter and generator are sized at the running load times this margin.

how: Your list runs {{out.running_w|int}} W at once ({{out.peak_w|int}} W when the biggest motor starts) and uses {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units a day, {{out.monthly_units|int}} a month. Inverter: the larger of {{out.running_w|int}} W × {{in.margin|2}} = {{out.inverter_kw_load|2}} kW and the solar array ÷ {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} = {{out.inverter_kw_array|2}} kW (an inverter accepts panels up to about that many times its rating), so {{out.inverter_kw|up1}} kW. Battery: {{in.backup_w}} W × {{in.backup_hours|1}} h = {{out.backup_kwh|2}} kWh ÷ ({{out.battery_v}} V × {{out.battery_dod|pct}} usable × {{d.inverter_eff_hybrid|pct}} inverter) = {{out.battery_ah|up}} Ah. Solar: energy {{out.daily_kwh|1}} kWh ÷ {{out.city_yield|1}} kWh per kW per day = {{out.solar_kw_energy|2}} kW; midday power {{out.running_w|int}} W ÷ {{out.pr|2}} performance ratio = {{out.solar_kw_power|2}} kW; the larger, {{out.solar_kw|2}} kW, needs {{out.panels|int}} panels of {{out.panel_w|int}} W = {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW making about {{out.monthly_solar_kwh|int}} units a month. Net billing counts an array up to your {{out.sanctioned_kw|1}} kW sanctioned load: {{out.net_billing_panels|int}} panels, {{out.net_billing_kw|2}} kW, about {{out.net_billing_solar_kwh|int}} units a month. You use {{out.self_used_units|int}} of those units yourself, export {{out.export_units|int}} at {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} and import {{out.import_units|int}}; energy charge {{out.bill_before_rs|rs}} before solar, {{out.bill_after_rs|rs}} after, saving {{out.saving_rs|rs}} a month on the energy charge alone. Generator for the whole list: {{out.generator_kva|1}} kVA, next standard size {{out.generator_pick_kva|1}} kVA.
